title: A Thing of Beauty
summary: In this extract from his long poem Endymion, John Keats declares that a beautiful thing gives lasting joy: its loveliness grows and never fades into nothingness. Despite the sorrows, disappointments and gloom of human life, beautiful things in nature and in great stories lift the spirit like an endless fountain of nectar flowing from heaven.

notes.heading: About the poet
notes.html: John Keats (1795–1821) was an English Romantic poet who died young of tuberculosis. His odes and narrative poems celebrate beauty, imagination and the senses. This extract is the opening of Endymion: A Poetic Romance (1818).

notes.heading: Gist
notes.html: Keats says that beauty is a permanent source of joy. Its charm increases with time and it gives us peace, good health and calm sleep. Every day we weave a bond of flowers to tie ourselves to the earth, in spite of despondency, the lack of noble people, gloomy days and dark paths. Beautiful things, the sun, moon, trees, daffodils, clear streams, forest thickets with musk-roses, and the stories of the mighty dead, remove the gloom from our spirits. They are like an endless fountain of immortal drink pouring from heaven.

notes.heading: Stanza-wise explanation (paraphrase)
notes.html:
Lines 1–5: Beauty is eternal. A beautiful thing is a joy for ever. Its loveliness keeps increasing and will never pass into nothingness. It keeps a quiet shelter, a bower, for us, giving sweet dreams, health and peaceful breathing.

Lines 6–13: Beauty as a bond with the earth. Every morning we weave a wreath of flowers that binds us to the earth. We need it because life is full of despair, there is a shortage of noble natures, we face gloomy days and unhealthy, dark paths in our search. Yet some shape of beauty removes the dark cloud from our spirits.

Lines 13–21: Sources of beauty. Such beautiful things include the sun and moon, old and young trees that provide shade to simple sheep, daffodils with the green world they live in, clear streams that make a cool covering for themselves against the hot season, and forest thickets rich with musk-rose blossoms. Also beautiful are the grand fates imagined for the mighty dead and the lovely tales we have heard or read.

Lines 22–24: The fountain of joy. All these are like an endless fountain of immortal drink, pouring onto us from the edge of heaven.

notes.heading: Poetic devices
notes.html:
• Metaphor: beauty as a ‘bower’ (a shady shelter), the ‘flowery band’ binding us to earth, and the ‘endless fountain’ of nectar.
  • Imagery: rich sensory pictures of sheep in shade, daffodils, rills and musk-roses.
  • Alliteration: repeated consonant sounds in phrases about sleep, health and breathing.
  • Rhyme scheme: rhyming couplets (heroic couplets) in iambic pentameter.
  • Inversion: unusual word order for rhythm and emphasis.
  • Contrast: the joy of beauty versus the gloom and suffering of life.
  • Enjambment: lines run on to the next without pause.

notes.heading: Themes
notes.html:
• Permanence of beauty: beauty never fades; it grows.
  • Beauty as consolation: it heals the suffering and despair of life.
  • Nature as a source of joy: the Romantic love of nature.
  • Imagination and art: great stories of heroes are also beautiful and immortal.

notes.heading: Title justification
notes.html: The title is taken from the opening phrase, which states the central idea of the poem: that a thing of beauty is a lasting joy. The entire extract elaborates what beautiful things are and how they help humanity.

notes.heading: Message and values
notes.html: We should seek, value and preserve beauty in nature and art, because it sustains us through hardship and gives our lives meaning and hope.

keyTerms.definition: A shady, leafy shelter in a garden; a metaphor for the comfort beauty provides.
Low spirits caused by loss of hope.
Weaving or twisting into a garland.
A thicket or dense growth of bushes in the forest.
Here, the grand destinies or fates of the mighty dead.
A pair of rhyming lines in iambic pentameter; the form of this poem.
An implied comparison, e.g. beauty as an endless fountain of immortal drink.

mcqs.q: From which longer work is ‘A Thing of Beauty’ taken?
mcqs.explanation: The extract is the opening of Keats’s Endymion.

mcqs.q: According to the poet, what happens to the loveliness of a beautiful thing over time?
mcqs.explanation: Keats says its loveliness increases and never passes into nothingness.

mcqs.q: What does the ‘flowery band’ bind us to?
mcqs.explanation: We weave a flowery band that binds us to the earth, giving us reasons to live.

mcqs.q: Which of these is NOT listed by the poet as a cause of human suffering?
mcqs.explanation: Keats mentions despair, scarcity of noble people, gloomy days and dark paths, but not wealth.

mcqs.q: What does a thing of beauty do to the ‘pall’ over our spirits?
mcqs.explanation: Beauty moves away the dark cloud of sadness from our spirits.

mcqs.q: The rills make a cooling covert for themselves against:
mcqs.explanation: Clear streams make a cool shelter against the hot season.

mcqs.q: The ‘endless fountain of immortal drink’ is a metaphor for:
options: the inexhaustible joy given by beautiful things
mcqs.explanation: Beautiful things give never-ending joy, like nectar from heaven.

mcqs.q: What is the rhyme scheme of the poem?
mcqs.explanation: The poem is written in rhyming couplets, i.e. heroic couplets.

mcqs.q: Why does the poet mention the ‘grandeur of the dooms’ of the mighty dead?
options: To show that stories of great people are also things of beauty
mcqs.explanation: Inspiring tales of heroes uplift us and are counted among beautiful things.

mcqs.q: Keats belonged to which literary movement?
mcqs.explanation: Keats was a Romantic poet who celebrated beauty, nature and imagination.

questions.q:
Read the situation and answer: The poet admits that life is full of sorrow, with a shortage of noble people and dark, unhealthy paths, yet a beautiful shape removes the gloom from our spirits.
(a) What are any two sources of human sorrow mentioned? (1)
(b) What removes the gloom? (1)
(c) What is the ‘pall’ a metaphor for? (1)
(d) What mood does this part convey? (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Despondency and lack of noble natures (also gloomy days, dark paths).

(b) Some shape or thing of beauty.

(c) Sadness and despair that cover the spirit like a dark cloth.

(d) A mood that moves from gloom to hope.

questions.q: Why is a thing of beauty a joy for ever?
questions.answerHtml: A beautiful thing gives lasting happiness. Its loveliness increases with time and never fades into nothingness. It provides peace, sweet dreams and health, and even its memory lifts our spirits in times of sorrow, so its joy is eternal.

questions.q: What is the ‘flowery band’ that binds us to the earth?
questions.answerHtml: The flowery band is a metaphor for the beautiful things around us. Every day these give us reasons to love life. They keep us attached to the earth despite pain and disappointment, just as a garland ties us with its fragrance.

questions.q: What image does the poet use to describe the beauty of nature and stories in the last lines?
questions.answerHtml: The poet describes them as an endless fountain of immortal drink pouring from heaven’s edge. The image shows that beauty is divine, inexhaustible and life-giving, like nectar that refreshes the soul and gives eternal joy.

questions.q: How does Keats suggest that beauty helps human beings bear the suffering of life? (120–150 words)
questions.answerHtml:
Keats openly accepts that life is full of suffering. People face despondency, there is a shortage of noble and kind natures, days are often gloomy, and the paths of life are dark and unhealthy. In such a world, people could easily lose hope.

Yet, the poet argues, beauty rescues us. A thing of beauty is a joy for ever; its charm grows and never dies. Like a shady bower, it gives rest, peaceful sleep and good health. Every day we weave a wreath of beautiful things that binds us to life. The sun, the moon, trees, daffodils, cool streams and musk-roses, and the inspiring tales of great men, remove the dark pall from our spirits.

These beautiful things are like an endless fountain of nectar from heaven, providing constant comfort. Thus beauty, for Keats, is a healing force that makes the burden of existence bearable.

questions.q: List the things of beauty mentioned in the poem and explain why the poet considers them a source of joy. (120–150 words)
questions.answerHtml:
Keats mentions many things of beauty. In nature there are the sun and moon, which shine on all; old and young trees that provide shade for simple sheep; daffodils surrounded by green; clear streams that create a cool shelter for themselves in summer; and forest thickets rich with musk-roses. In human culture there are the grand stories of the mighty dead and the lovely tales we have heard or read.

He considers them sources of joy because their beauty is permanent and increasing. They provide a quiet bower of peace, health and sweet dreams. They bind us to the earth through a flowery band and lift the dark cloud of sadness from our spirits.

Most importantly, they are inexhaustible. Keats compares them to an endless fountain of immortal drink pouring from heaven. Their joy is spiritual and divine, refreshing human beings throughout their lives.
